note: Reading the LIVE artifact instead of the code's claims about it inverts the priority order. The code says 76 Q-keys and an adaptive alpha that makes volatile keys learn faster. The file says 29 of 76 keys are pinned within 1e-5 of the clip, and that the previous save had 3. Saturation went 4% -> 38% inside one process lifetime. Neither number is visible from the source. Rule: for any subsystem with a persisted table, measure the table first and read the code second, because the table accumulates the consequences of every past decision and the code only shows the current one.

Derivation: adaptive_alpha = clamp(0.2*(1+min(2,sqrt(var)*2)), 0.05, 0.5). Default variance for an unmeasured key is 0.25 -> alpha 0.4. From neutral, q reaches 0.99999 in 22 pulls. The live keys carry 21-31 pulls. The arithmetic and the data agree to the pull, which is what makes this a measurement rather than a hypothesis. The inferred step: the feature that selects a HIGHER alpha for high variance drives those keys to the clip SOONER, and the clip is a state in which a key can no longer express the variance that selected the alpha. The mechanism built to make volatile keys responsive is the mechanism that erases them. Generalised: an adaptive parameter whose target state is absorbing will select for the very inputs it was designed to handle, and then destroy their signal.

Two routes carry 30 failures each at EXACTLY 8000.0ms. 8000ms is not a duration, it is a timeout constant, and the timeout was caused by sync_wsl_to_kali's doubled path -- fixed in commit 56c15679, the day before. So the penalty outlives its cause. The structural argument that makes it worse than stale: a deprioritised route is never re-chosen, so it never produces the successes that would clear it. The penalty is self-sustaining. Then the deeper read: the module's own get_q_updates docstring already names this failure mode for NEVER-TRIED arms and fixes it with a pull count. That is one half of the problem and it was solved. The other half -- TRIED-THEN-BROKEN-THEN-FIXED -- is strictly worse, because a never-tried arm scores neutral 0 and needs a chance while a fixed arm carries a negative score that is exactly as stale as the bug. The two halves look like one problem and are not, which is why one was solved and the other was invisible.

The conftest fixture reasons correctly -- 'a test must not be able to damage the machine it is testing' -- and then stops at the boundary. Containment prevents NEW damage; it says nothing about EXISTING damage, and it leaves the evidence of past damage indistinguishable from production data. The missing third leg is PROVENANCE. Verified on the live store: 14 fixture keys in the same namespaces as production worms, including mesh:T0/T1/T2 at -0.9217/+0.9217/+0.9217, an exact mirrored triple which is a fixture signature if anything is. Correction I had to make mid-analysis: a name-shape heuristic flagged diagnostic:ChaosWorm and learning:EvolutionEngine as fabricated because they had no pull count. Both are real worms. And a 'not in WORM_REGISTRY' probe over-flags 48 keys, because synapse:/route:/aoa_route:/monitor: key on EDGES and SITES. So the classification is DECLARED, not inferred, and the rot-check asserts only the witnessed subset -- because mesh:T0/T1/T2 are ORPHANED (no test or script creates them) and a check demanding a living fixture for every declared name would have failed instead of documenting that.

Six keys carry a weight with no pull count AND no variance. git log -S puts the count table and the payload field in the same commit (e67c5f6d) as the test isolation -- i.e. a field was added to a PERSISTED SCHEMA in the same change that started writing it, with no backfill for rows that already existed, and __version__ never moved. The consequence is sharper than data loss: the two routes with the most successes in the system (windows>windows at 27, g_archive at 32) reported a pull count of ZERO, so the one API built to distinguish 'proven neutral' from 'never measured' returned 'never measured' for the best-evidenced keys in the table. A schema change with no backfill does not lose data, it RELABELS it, which is worse, because the consumer cannot tell the label is a lie. The repair was a re-derivation, not a guess: successes+failures sat in the homeostat the whole time. Observed running in production: 0 -> 27 and 0 -> 32.

THE finding. Live synapse table: 31 edges, 3 distinct values, 25 of them at exactly +0.0909. Root cause: SynapseWeightWorm.update computes td_error = r + gamma*V(s') - V(s), a DELTA, and passes it as reward=, which the brainstem applies as a TARGET (q += alpha*(reward - q), i.e. q converges TO reward). So q was dragged toward lr*td_error instead of accumulating it. The two caller families are wrong in OPPOSITE directions from one cause: sign callers pass +-1 as a target and SATURATE at the clip in 22 pulls; the TD caller passes a small delta as a target and COLLAPSES to ~0.09. The table was simultaneously saturated and flat. The decisive detail: record_outcome's own docstring said 'callers that computed a real learning signal (a TD error, a shaped reward) pass it here so magnitude survives the hand-off' -- it advertised DELTA semantics while the implementation applied TARGET semantics. Both call sites read a different half of the same sentence and neither was wrong about the half it read. Generalised: when a parameter's meaning is described in prose but not distinguished by the API, two callers will disagree about it, and each will be locally correct. The fix is to name the operation, not to reshape the number.

I wrote a regression test for G6 that passed on the PRE-FIX source. Distinctness is not the discriminator: with distinct rewards BOTH conventions keep the edges distinct, so an assertion of distinctness is satisfied by the defect. I only found this by deliberately reverting the fix and running it -- which is the whole reason to do that step rather than assume it. The real discriminator is MAGNITUDE, because the conventions have different fixed points: delta -> reward (0.4000), target -> lr*r/(1+lr) (0.0364), an 11x underestimate. That is exactly the live signature: edges holding ~0.09 where their outcomes implied far more. Same trap as the previous audit's probes, where four of twenty-one were false-positive generators. Rule: a test that passes on the broken code is not a test of the fix, and the only way to know is to break the code on purpose.

Two pre-existing tests failed after the change and neither was noise. test_q_order_preserves_ordering_semantics builds a reference implementation of the sort and pins the KEY in it -- so a key change legitimately fails it, and updating the reference is correct while updating the expectation blindly would not be. It guards an O(n^2) -> O(n log n) rewrite, not a key. test_every_unreferenced_function_is_declared correctly demanded wire-or-cut decisions for the new functions; the tool reported them and one of them (get_q_effective) disappeared from the list once I wired it into the RL card rather than declaring it wired while nothing called it. Recorded because 'the test is stale' and 'the test is right' look identical at the moment they go red, and the difference is whether the assertion is about a CONTRACT or about an IMPLEMENTATION.

Consolidating duplicate formulas is a correctness fix, not a tidiness fix. clamp(base_w * (1 + q), 0.1, 5.0) appeared in TWO files with identical text, which is how two docstrings came to advertise the same unreachable range: with q in [-1,1] the factor is [0,2], so for the only registered base_w the ceiling is 2.0 and the declared 5.0 is unreachable in every live call site. Neither copy was wrong on its own; the pair was. One implementation (route_weight) plus a DERIVED range (route_weight_range) makes the claim self-checking, and a test now asserts the declared ceiling is reachable only by an input the brainstem cannot produce.

Three of the fixes converge on one idea worth naming: a stored value and the EVIDENCE behind it are different quantities and must travel together. Route weight 0.667 and route weight 0.667-from-4-observations are different claims; the router could only see the first. Raw q at the clip and raw q at the clip on 10 vs 31 pulls are different claims; q_order could only see the first. A pull count of 0 because the key was measured zero times, and a pull count of 0 because a schema migration erased it, are different claims; get_q_updates could only see the first. In all three cases the fix was to make the evidence part of the value's representation rather than a separate lookup a caller must remember to do. Shrinkage q*n/(n+K) is the compact form of that: it is a single number that cannot be read without its evidence.
